Mr. Speaker, before this Bill is read a third time, I desire to say a few words on behalf of certain members of the order with regard to which this Bill purports to legislate, who have brought several matters to my notice, asking that I should bring them to the attention of parliament. In the first place, I will say that when I first received an intimation that some of the members of the order objected to this legislation, I went to the hon. member (Mr. Heyd) who has charge of the Bill, and I gave him a copy of the documents which have been placed in my hands, asking that the High Court of the Older of Foresters should send some one to the district where these objecting members are, to see if their objections could not be removed. I have received information for them within the last two or three days, to say that nothing of this kind had been done, and desiring me to bring their objections before the House. I regret exceedingly that owing to the pi-ess of work I was unable to attend the committee to present these objections. Therefore, I purpose to move to-night that the Bill be not now read a third time, but that it be referred back to the Committee on Banking and Commerce for further consideration. I may say in the first place, that the notice given for this Bill was very short indeed. The only intimation that the members of the lodges had that any legislation of this character was being sought, was by a circular dated the 2nd of April. There was not the usual notice given. There was no notice given in the paper, and the only notice, as I understand. that the members of the Foresters order had, was by a circular sent out from the House of Commons, dated the 2nd of April. I may say almost immediately after that circular was sent out, i received the following resolution :
Subsidiary High Court of Canada,
Ancient Order of Foresters,
April 9th, 1901.
Court Brighton.

Hyman, Esq., M.P.
Dear Sir,-At a regular meeting of the above court, held in their hall, Sraig street, this April 9th, the inclosed notice was read.
That refers to the notice that was sent out from the House of Commons, containing the provisions of the Bill.
And it was resolved that as a court, we request you, as member from London, to use your influence to prevent the passage of this same Bill, as per inclosed notice. For thi3 reason : the attempt was made in Toronto and they had to make an amendment directly stating that no interference could be made with funds of any subordinate court.
I understand, Sir, that since the Bill was introduced, an amendment of that character has been incorporated in it, but 1 also desire to say that these gentlemen who.
through me are petitioning that this Bill should go back to the committee, are not yet satisfied. The resolution continues :
That they state in this circular that this Bill will not affect our funds in subordinate courts, is no assurance to us, as they have overstepped the powers granted them already, and we have no confidence in them. The powers of the extreme council of the high court are for carrying out measures prescribed by the delegates in high court assemblies between meetings of the high court, and they had a right to first lay before the assembled delegates in high court the Bill they are trying to get passed at Ottawa ; thus, we consider their object in obtaining such powers so as to be able to override the courts of the order. They have already put themselves, by their actions, largely in debt, and although at the high court meeting in August, 1899, the delegates gave them an increase in the sick and funeral fund of $2,100 per year, and in the management fund $1,800, yet according^ to their last audit they show no decrease in their indebtedness. Thus, you see, we have good reason to regard their present action with suspicion.
Done on behalf of the court, which, I might say, numbers over 170 members and have been doing good work in London South since its organization in August, 1880.
JOHN G. ORCHARD, Chief Ranger.
CHAS. FINCHAMP, Sub-Ranger.
WM. ROW, Treasurer.
HY. SUTHERLAND, Secretary.
I may say that In addition to that, on the Otli of April I received the following :
London, Ont., April 9, 1901. Sir, I have taken the liberty of sending you the inclosed resolution, trusting you will use your best endeavours to defeat the Ancient Order of Foresters' Bill when it is brought before the committee, or in the House, in behalf of 1,400 members of Middlesex district.

. District Chief Ranger.
Moved by Bro. Peter Todd, P.D.C.R., seconded by Bro. R. W. Timson :
That this meeting of the members of the Ancient Order of Foresters of the Middlesex district, assembled at London, Ont., this 8th day of April, 1901, are of unanimous opinion that no further legislation should be applied for on behalf of the Ancient Order of Foresters until after the views of the members of the order are obtained at the next high court meeting is held in August, 1901, and that a copy of this resolution be forwarded to Bro. Mills, High Chief Ranger, and the members of the Dominion parliament representing the city of London and the county of Middlesex. '

D.C.R., Middlesex district.
I wrote to the members of the order who had been corresponding with me, telling them that I had spoken to the lion, gentleman who had charge of the Bill, asking that some deputation or some high officer of the order be sent to discuss the matter. This, however, was not done, and I am la receipt of the following :-

London, April 13, 1901. Charles Hyman, Esq., M.P.,
Dear Sir,-Yours just to hand re A. O. F. Bill.
I might say on behalf of the Middlesex district that no explanations from the officers can satisfy the members of this district.

Heyd, our high court solicitor, has asked the House of Commons, on behalf of an applicant, to have this Bill passed. The Ancient Order of Foresters has no one-man power; at each of our bi-annual meetings the representatives of the subordinate courts elect an executive body to transact our business, and the said representatives make rules for their guidance. This executive body has not met to instruct our high court solicitor to ask for such a Bill; even if they had met and instructed him to do so, they would be exceeding their duty. From information we have received the Independent Order of Foresters, not the Canadian order, got into the same trouble and asked for legislation. The Independent Order is an insurance society first, and sick benefits if a member wishes to take such benefits. The Ancient Order of Foresters is a sick benefit society first, and insurance if a member wishes to accept it. There are abount one thousand members in our order in Canada that have taken insurance, the remaining 12,000 have sick benefits only. If there is legislation required, the various subordinate courts should have been consulted, or, in other words, we say our high court meets next August, then if legislation is required the delegates will say whether it is required or not. This same Bill, or a similar one, was asked for by the same person at this present session of the Ontario parliament, and their Bill was defeated.
I am told that is not so. I am informed that the gentleman is wrong in making that statement.
Petitions were sent in from different parts of the province asking the Bill not to pass for the same reason I have quoted. Not thinking that this Bill would have gone to Ottawa, or else copies would have been forwarded to Ottawa.
We trust that you will do your utmost to have the said Bill laid over or defeated until our high court meeting in'August next.
Yours very truly,
W. RICHARDS, D.C.R., Middlesex District.
This, Mr. Speaker, is all I have to say in the matter. Out of 12,000 or 13,000 members of the order, here is a protest coming from nearly 10 per cent, stating that they had not had proper notice of the legislation. Under the circumstances, it is only fair and just to give them an opportunity of expressing their views before the committee of the House. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Bast Middlesex (Mr. Gilmour), that the Bill be not now read a third time, but that it be referred back to the Committee on Banking and Commerce for further consideration.
ROSS (South Ontario), t am somewhat in the same position as my hon. friend from London (Mr. Hyman). I have no direct interest in the order, and I scarcely feel like putting myself on record against

the hon. member who is introducing this Bill, but I have a duty to discharge to one of my constituents, who has written me in connection with the matter, and I proprose to read some correspondence I have had from him. He writes me :
The executive council of this order, it would appear, has of late been assuming the right, in the name of the subsidiary high court, to secure legislation along such lines as it chooses. The constitution and by-laws ot the subsidiary high court do not confer any right or power to the executive council to legislate on behalf of the order.
At this session of the legislature of Ontario, the executive council made an attempt to push through a Bill giving the council power to take over and to control all the ' assets, rights, credits, effects and property, real, personal and mixed, of whatsoever kind and wheresoever situate,' practically stripping the subordinate branches of the order of everything they possessed, but prompt action and opposition to the Bill before the committee of the House secured to the subordinate courts a saving clause which, I understand, has been added to the Bill.
For your information, I may state that there are two classes of members in the order, those who enter for sick and funeral benefits only, and those who are connected with the order for the sick and funeral benefits plus any insurance they may wish to take, from $250 up to $2,000. Many of the subordinate courts, through choice, are working along the benevolent and fraternal lines of the order, their members not desiring or choosing to take out insurance in the order, and these courts, through care and judicious management, have to their credit considerable sums, prudently safeguarded, for their use in the event of an epidemic or jiny unusual distress amongst their members, and as a matter of course they are averse to their funds being confiscated and taken over under the management of others.
Should a Bill similar to the one introduced to the Ontario legislature appear in the Dominion House. I trust a saving clause may be added to it, protecting the funds and properties of the subordinate courts.
He writes again on the 25th of April. I have sent him a copy of the Bill and all the information I could obtain on tlie matter ; and he assures me in the second letter that the Bill is not all right. He says ;
The assurances which you have that the Bill is all right, are not. reliable, and must come from the promoters of the Bill. The Bill is not all right, as you will plainly see by comparing it with the Ontario Bill, a copy of which I sent you a week ago or more. The Ontario Bill was amended in committee by the addition of two clauses, Nos. 5 and 6.
Our court held a meeting last night, and the court members were very anxious that the Bill shall be held over until after the high court meeting, which will take place in about three months; and if it cannot be done, it is desirable and necessary that a clause shall be added to it similar to that which was, added to the Ontario Bill. If the Bill, as its promoters claim, is all right, and it is not its aim to confiscate the funds of the subordinate courts, there can I be no harm done in having the saving clauses I added.

I just give you the ideas of this particular court, which is situated in my constituency. I know nothing of the Bill, but X am assured by the promoter that some of these matters have been arranged, and I would be glad to have him state that they have all been arranged.

I have received a letter from the secretary of the Ancient Order of Foresters, in St. Thomas, bearing on the same points, and asking for the same provisions that have been asked for by the hon. member for London (Mr. Hyman), and the hon. member for South Ontario (Mr. Ross).

When this Bill was before the committee I objected to it on similar grounds ; but, on being assured by the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Heyd) that there was no objection to the Bill, I allowed it to go through. But, 1 raised the same objection in the House. It occurred to me that if such legislation was necessary, it should first be submitted to the subordinate courts, to be dealt with by them. Then, they would know what was being done. But this Bill was being hurried through without the usual delays or notice.
There appears to be a tremendous amount of wilful ignorance, as well as misrepresentation, in regard to this Bill.

Is that parliamentary ?
Mr. HEY'D. I would not accuse any member of this House of misrepresentation, but the information which some hon. members have got is false. This Bill is quite simple, and in the oxiinion of the High Court, is absolutely necessary. This legislation was applied for, not by a person, but by the High Court, which is authorized to make the application. The Bill was introduced into the Ontario legislature shortly before it was introduced here. About fifty delegates attended there to ascertain the nature of the Bill, and, having ascertained what it was, they unanimously supported it, and it passed through the local House, and has become law in the province. The clause which my hon. friend from South Ontario alluded to, guaranteeing not to interfere with the funds belonging to the subsidiary courts, was added in the Ontario House, and the same clause was introduced into this Bill at the meeting of the committee. Therefore, the Bill which we have before us is exactly the same as the Bill which unanimously passed through the local House, after having been discussed by the members of the order who were there, and who went away satisfied with it. Now, what does the High Court ask for ? Some twenty years ago the Ancient Order of Foresters got a provincial charter as a friendly society. They added to it an Insurance branch. To this about 10 per cent of
the members belong. In 1S97, the legislature of Quebec passed an Act requiring all friendly societies doing business in that province and not having a Dominion charter, to deposit $5,000 in money. The membership belonging to the insurance part ol' the order being very small, the $5,000, compared with the total assets of the society, was very large, and the High Court thought it would be cheaper to get a Dominion charter than to deposit $5,000. In 1898, the High Court applied for a Dominion charter and obtained it, and their action was ratified at a subsequent meeting of the High Court, and they have been doing business under their Dominion charter ever since. Recently, In Manitoba, a suit was instituted against the Independent Order of Foresters, who had a charter similar to ours ; and they discovered that it was defective, in so far as it did not pass the membership belonging to the provincial lodge over to the Dominion Grand Lodge. The suit was compromised. The Independent Order of Foresters came down here and got supplementary legislation to remove the difficulty. That legislation passed this House unanimously. The Ancient Order of Foresters detected the same defect in their legislation, and they have come down here with a facsimile of the Bill of the Independent Order of Foresters, word for word, in the first four clauses, and they ask that it be passed. No harm can happen to a single individual belonging to the Ancient Order of Foresters. The executive committee, who represent all these courts, think this legislation is absolutely necessary in order to preserve the funds of the society; and the letters read here to-night are written under an entire misapprehension of the scope of this Bill. In order to remove any objections which might exist, a clause was inserted in the Bill when it was before the committee, similar to that which was asked for in the Ontario legislature, and there unanimously accepted. The Bill does not affect the finances of the subordinate courts. It is asked for by the accredited representatives of the order. I myself am one of the High Court trustees, Mr. Clarke, of West Toronto, is another ; two out of the three being members of this House : and, together with the executive committee, we ask that this legislation be passed in the interest of the Ancient Order of Foresters. There cannot be any objection to it. When the Bill came before the committee these letters were read ; and in order to give people who might be opposed to the legislation an opportunity to make themselves heard, we postponed the action of the committee to a subsequent date; and, as I predicted at the time, there was not a man there to raise his voice against it. These letters are read by hon. gentlemen to show their constituents that they are not neglecting their interests ; but, so far as they afford a valid objection to this Bill, there is nothing in them. To say that the courts had not suffl-

cient notification is absurd. They had sufficient to enable them to carry the matter through the provincial courts ; and in order to give them more information still, a circular letter was addressed to every court in this country, and we have answers from nearly 200, of whom only two or three make any objections. In the face of such a unanimous request from the order, in the face of this request from the officers of the order and its trustees, it strikes me that the objections urged by two or three people should not have any weight in this House.

Upon representations made to me personally, as also by letters, such as the hon. member for London (Mr. Hyman) has just read, I feel called upon to support this amendment. The hon. member for South Brant (Mr. Heyd) says there is nothing in these representations and that they are the result of an entire misapprehension of the proposed legislation. It is possible that the hon. gentleman, is correct, but, if any misapprehension exists it is because the subsidiary bodies have never been consulted as they should have been. As I understand that body, of which I am not a member, I think, after reading the preamble, that the petitioners are quite right iu their objection. In the first place, there existed the Ancient Order of Foresters, incorporated by the provincial House in the year 1877. This continued in operation until the 30th of June, 1898, when it ceased existence and the Dominion Order of Foresters was incorporated by Royal assent. And on that date, the Dominion Order of Foresters, apparently without any authority other than the decision of its executive, assumed all the contracts and liabilities of the provincial corporation, performed all its duties and fulfilled all its obligations as they matured; and having done this without any authority from the subordinate body, the Dominion Order asks this parliament to enact as follows :
2. The Dominion corporation defined in the preamble shall be deemed to have had the authority on the 13th day of June, 1898, to accept, and^ shall he deemed to have accepted on the said date, a transfer to the Dominion corporation. its successors and assigns, to its and their own use absolutely, of all the assets, interests, rights, effects and property, real, personal and mixed, of whatever kind and wherever situate belonging to the provincial corporation, also defined in the preamble, or to which the provincial corporation was, is or shall hereafter be entitled.
I do not think this parliament should step In between the executive and the subsidiary lodges and declare that the executive laid the right to make such an arrangement for the purchase of the assets and the redemption of the liabilities of any other body.
It has been stated by the hon. member for Brant that two amendments were introduced in the local legislature and have been added to this Bill, the effect of which is to relieve the subordinate body of any responsibility

or liability by reason of this High Court taking over all the assets and liabilities of the provincial corporation. But this amendment will not apply to the individual members of the lodges who hold a certificate of insurance from the High Court and not from the subordinate lodges. This taking hold of those assets and paying off those liabilities, whether it may have good or evil effect, will affect every one of those individuals who hold this insurance. This being the case, and the subsidiary courts not having been consulted, we should not pass this legislation. It seems that the High Court holds bi-annual meetings to which the subordinate courts send delegates, who there consult with regard to any legislation or bylaws required, but that has not been done in this instance. The High Court has never consulted the subordinate lodges about this legislation, and I maintain that the latter should be consulted and be put in a position to make their representations here. If they are under a misapprehension as regards this legislation, that is not to be Wondered at as they never received notice of it. I will, Mr. Speaker, second the amendment moved by the hon. member for London.

Let me read the two clauses which are added to the Bill :
Nothing in this Act contained shall be deemed to affect or interfere with the funds or assets of the subordinate courts.
Nothing in this Act contained shall prejudice the right of any plaintiff in any action now pending to make any claim now open to him, but he shall have the same right thereto as if this Act had not been passed.
The effect in the legislation is this. The Dominion Grand lodge have the funds and are carrying on the business, while the members that belong to the insurance branch of the order think they have not been regularly transferred. While they have the money they have not got the old members, and it is to put these old members right, they are asking for this legislation.
While as the subordinate lodges or their funds may not be effected, the individual members of the order, holding their insurance from the high court, will be affected.

I would like to call attention to one fact not mentioned, and that is that this legislation asked by the High Court of the Ancient Order of Foresters is in every respect the same as that passed this session on behalf of the Supreme Court of the Independent Order of Foresters. Bill No. 6. This shows that the condition of these two great bodies was precisely the same as regards their power under the provincial Act, and the powers subsequently assumed under the Dominion Act. It is not intended, in the slightest degree, to interfere with the fund or organization of the subsidiary bodies, but simply to carry out the scheme already agreed to by ail

the subsidiary bodies and which has been in actual operation quite a long time. The provincial body had transferred all its assets and liabilities to the same body, subsequently incorporated under a Dominion Act. The same situation as exists in this case was found to have existed with regard to the Independent Order of Foresters, and the Bill dealing with the latter was passed by this House without objection. The presumption is that there should not have been anything in it prejudicial to the members of the subsidiary courts. Otherwise, we would have had objection similar to that taken on behalf of some of the subsidiary bodies of the Independent Order of Foresters. I took considerable pains to understand this Bill and to talk with the counsel who was here, and I am strongly of opinion that the Act asked for here is almost purely of a technical nature and does not in the slightest degree Interfere -with the control of the funds or any substantial interests of the members of the order.
Is the object of the proposed amendment to enable these parties to be heard before a committee
Yes.
If you postpone it you will not have a soul in committee. We tried that once before.

I think I must accept the suggestion of my hon. friend from London (Mr. Hyman), that these gentlemen desire to be heard before the committee. if upon his responsibility he informs the House that such is the object of his motion. I would remind the House that the Bill came before us under exceptional circumstances. On the 1st of April my hon. friend from South Brant (Mr. ITeyd) moved that the 49th rule, limiting the time for petitions for private Bills, should be suspended. And I would infer that this Bill had not received the ordinary notice given of private Bills through the medium of the press. Am I right ?
Yes.

Then, I would suggest to my hon. friend from South Brant that if gentlemen interested in the association desire to be heard before the committee, an opportunity should be afforded them. Certainly, their request to be heard is entitled to more consideration than if the usual notice had been given of this Bill and the Bill had received the assent of the subordinate lodges. When the directors of a corporation come here with a Bill affecting the interests of the shareholders, the House refuses to pass the legislation except subject to the proviso that it shall receive the assent of the shareholders at a general meeting. This Bill has not received the assent of the subordinate lodges, as I understand it, and I think it only fair that those lodges
should be allowed an opportunity to be heard before committee.

If the clauses added to this Bill on Friday last were not acceptable to the members of the order, I would strongly support the proposition of the hon. member for London, that further delay should be granted. I have had a great deal of correspondence with the members of the order in Toronto, the city where the order was first established in Canada, and where it has hundreds, if not thousands, of members. After correspondence with these brethren, and after sending them a copy of the Bill as it was amended last Friday, I received the following communication :
I heartily thank you for your favour received to-day of Bill as amended. They are the same clauses, which we had inserted in the local Bill, referred to in my letter to you of yesterday, and that removes any opposition that has been shown to the Bill as we believe the added clauses clearly define the position of subordinate courts, re their surplus funds.
Accept the thanks of myself and 'the 'brethren of the city who have shown interest in the Bill, and who are now quite satisfied with the Bill as it stands.
With be3t regards,
Yours truly,

E. F. Clarke, Esq., M. P.
Mr. Williams is one of the oldest and most earnest and indefatigable workers in the order in the province of Ontario, a gentleman who lias occupied almost every position in the order. The fear that was entertained by the brethren has been removed by the action of the committee, prompted by my hon. friend from South Brant, by the insertion of sections protecting the funds of tile subordinate lodges. Their interests are absolutely secure, as I believe and am advised, under the Bill before the House. Under these circumstances, I hope tfhe objection will be withdrawn and the Bill passed to-night. I am satisfied the brethren are labouring under a misapprehension as to the powers given, and I am satisfied the funds of the subordinate lodges are protected by the amendments made in committee.

After hearing the statement of my hon. friend from South Brant and that of the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Clarke), who is one of the trustees, I understand, of this association, it may be that the objectors are labouring under a misapprehension. But, for the sake of peace and harmony and to satisfy these people, I would suggest to my hon. friend (Mr. Heyd) that it would be better to accept the motion and to refer the matter to the committee. It would only delay the measure for a few days; and, when these people find that objections have been removed by the amendments, that will create a better feeling and be to the advantage of all concerned.

I have no objection to delay it for any length of time, if there is no danger of it lapsing to the prorogation of parliament. If my hon. friend from London (Mr. Hyman) will agree to have the objectors here next Wednesday, I will accept the amendment.

If the hon. gentleman (Mr. Heyd) will accept the motion. I will undertake at once to send the amendment to these parties. I do not know whether they have had notice of them and whether the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Clarke) has had correspondence with these people in Middlesex
I sent the Bill this day week to the gentlemen who were objecting to it, and I have read the answer I received.
If the hon. member (Mr. Heyd) will accept my suggestion and will have the matter brought up in committee on Wednesday
We want to hear all the objections that can fairly be raised. We do not want to smuggle the Bill through the House.

Although entertaining this view about the matter, we are by no means disposed to counsel the Dominion parliament to undertake the task of saving Manitoba from herself. The legislature of that province, fresh as it is from the people, deliberately gave it.s sanction to these bargains, it was fully aware of the responsibilities which it assumed on behalf of the pro-yince. There is nothing to warrant us in treating the province as if incompetent to manage its own affairs. The only duty that lies on the Dominion parliament is to see that its own control over the railways which it has sub-ventioned and the control of the provinces which have granted aid on definite terms to some of these railways are not impaired by the legislation which is now asked for.
-there certainly is in that nothing very nattering to the parties in Manitoba who have made these deals. There has been no criticism of their Bills as railway Bills, because they are connected with a deal *which is all on the side of tile railway company. Whatever else may be accomplished whatever chances may be run, this, on the face of the contract, is assured, that for the next thirty years the Canadian Northern Railway Company have the key to the cash box ot Manitoba, and if they do not help themselves it will be more out of charity and honesty than for want of an opportunity. I do not remember seeing in the report of the Minister of the Interior that any great number of immigrants landed at these places, and I am surprised at seeing $5,500 for two buildings where there is only a small number of immigrants.
I know that district very well, and I can assure my hon. friend that immigrants are pouring into it rapidly at the present time.
Is it European immigration ?

Yes, and people are coming from the United States in large numbers. I believe that within the last few days 200 or 300 people went there.
Rideau Hall-To make good damage done by the fire of November 25, 1900, and putting In new concrete floors in stables in place of old wooden floors, &c., $5,000.
Who is putting in the concrete floors ?
Our own staff at Rideau Hall.
Where do you get the cement ?

We buy some at Montreal.
Paris, Ont.-Public Buildings-Governor General's warrant, $18,000.
What is the meaning of the Governor General's warrant ?

A fire destroyed the building and they had Mr. TARTE.
no money available, so we obtained a warrant. This will not complete the work.
Has the hon. minister received any application for a public building at St. Laurent ?

Yes, several people of both political parties applied for a public buildng there. If I have some little encouragement another year, I may be glad to try my hand at it.
Toronto Post Office

Extension of the Union station sorting room, elevator, tower hoist, &c., $12,000.
I understand that this money is to be expended on Grand Trunk Railway property.

There is an arrangement by which the Grand Trunk Railway pay us some interest on the money spent.
New Westminster, B.C., Public Building-Reconstruction, $10,000.
What is the total amount spent on New Westminster public building last year ?
$34,000 up to the 1st of January.
Will this finish it ?

Will require $10,000 more in the supplemen-taries. The work is under contract.
Telephone Service-Public Buildings, Ottawa, $2,350.

How much per telephone does the government pay ?
The MINISTER OF PUBLIC WrORKS. Thirty-five dollars.
How much is the main appropriation for telephone service ?

$5,000. We were behind on that appropriation from year to year, and we concluded to ask for an additional amount to pay up arrears.
Public Building, Ottawa-Fitting up offices over Molson Bank for Labour Department, including steam coils, &c., $4,000.
The MINISTER OF PUBLIC 'WORKS. This is the Labour Bureau on Metcalfe street. These are steel files run along the wall with places inside for papers.

There are many papers in some of the public departments, which represent a very large expenditure of money and are not adequately protected from fire. It would be worthy of consideration to see whether they could be protected.

When we had a fire in the West block, if

the department had been supplied with these steel files we would not have lost so many papers. In the supplementaries there Is a pretty large amount for steel files. We have most of the departments not protected as they should be.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
I moved some time ago for a return of all the buildings rented by the government.
The MINISTER OP PUBLIC [DOT] WORKS. I will bring down this paper early next week.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I am informed that the Inland Revenue Department have lately rented a building somewhere on Queen street near the market and that the laboratory has been moved to that building.
I know that the Inland Revenue Department has a building on Wellington street, but I do not remember any building of theirs on Queen street.
I do not know the name of the street, but it is a new building down near the market. The officers of the department have just moved in. I was there and saw the stuff there.

I am at a loss to know what the hon. gentleman means. My deputy does not seem to know anything about it, and neither do I. The building may have been rented by the department without my knowledge, though I should be surprised if that were done. Still, if they rent it and pay for it I would not object.
I understand that the rental is $1,200 a year.
Well. I will bring a complete list of the buildings that are rented here in Ottawa.
How many buildings in Ottawa are now rented by the various departments ?
There are thirteen buildings or parts of buildings rented.
Can the hon. gentleman give the committee an idea of the amount paid in rentals per year ?

Have the government considered the question of providing additional accommodation by the erection of a building, instead of providing room in this piecemeal way, and sometimes, apparently, being compelled to pay pretty high prices. It is well known that more accommodation is required in these very buildings for instance, the library needs more room, and more room is needed for the various purposes in connection with the House of
Commons and the Senate. It is apparent also that better accommodation is required for the various departments. One would think that a more business-like way would be to consider the advisability of erecting another building, and, if necessary, purchasing a site for that purpose.

The only additional accommodation provided for in my estimates is in connection with this House. I intend using part of the yard over the engine house. We can get there a space of about 40 by 00 feet. The building will afford us six additional rooms, and, in the top storey a large committee room 40 by 00 feet. If it was permitted me to speak not as a minister, but as a member of parliament pure and simple-
We will permit that for a few moments.
Especially the pure and simple.

I will take that permission, and I would entirely agree with the view expressed by the leader of the opposition. To my mind it is ridiculous to have so many departments and public offices scattered over the city. When I took office there were several buildings rented, and we have been obliged to rent others. [DOT] Instead of that, we should erect the public buildings that are necessary. The departments are cramped, and there is not an additional foot to be had. I have been all over the buildings with the chief architect, I do not know bow many times. But when a poor Minister of Public Works comes before his colleagues with an expenditure of two or three hundred thousand dollars in view, he becomes a public enemy; his budget is too large; he is an expensive man
Oh, oh.

I am only telling the gospel truth. The minister is told that the project is too large. That is my position so far. I am prepared to carry the blame, but I fully recognize that we should not go on, as my hon. friend (Mr. Borden, Halifax) says by this piecemeal method. It is a bad system. At the same time, I must say it is a difficult question to grapple with. First there is the question of site. Sites are pretty expensive in Ottawa. We are accused of paying, high rents. I am glad the question has come up, because the more it comes up the more it will help me to carry out the views that I think are right. We should have an additional building somewhere. There was in former days, and there is now some talk of a colonnade that would unite the buildings together. The chief architect, Mr. Ewart, who is a capable and most practical man, is giving his attention to this question now. I have not made up my mind as to the plans I

would advise my colleagues to adopt, but I fully recognize that we are not doing what we ought to do.

I am glad to hear the Minister of Public Works admit that the system which has been adopted by himself and his predecessors is not giving the satisfaction that the arrangement adopted should give. I think a suggestion might well be thrown out that the public buildings we now have might be used to a great deal better advantage than they now are. If the hon. minister were to go into the establishment of Armour & Co., or Swift & Co., of Chicago, he would find in one building the size of one of these, three times as many men as are in the whole of these buildings, and under the supervision of one man, he would probably learn how to place a lot of men without putting each man by himself into a room large enough to accommodate three or four men. The custom has been heretofore that, as soon as a man is required to look after any particular branch of a department, he gets room for himself and an assistant, and they shut themselves up in that room, and you do not know whether they are doing anything or not. The next man gets another room, 20 feet square for himself, and so on. So I think when the government are talking about erecting extra buildings in order to make extra space, they [DOT] would do well to adopt some business system whereby a greater number of employees may be grouped together and thus save a great deal of space. .

When the Langevin block was erected this very question came up, and Sir John A. Macdonald was of the opinion that a large number of employees could be grouped together in some big rooms. It is not necessary to go to Armour's place for an example; if you go to Montreal you will find the Canadian Pacific Railway and the Grand Trunk Railway Company have their employees in large rooms. Here the question has been settled in another way. I fully admit that the suggestion is worthy of consideration. There is no doubt that if a larger number of employees were in large rooms we could economize space to a great extent But those who preceded us and had experience, thought differently, and we have followed their example
5Ir. RICHARDSON (Lisgar). Has the minister ever thought of the idea of putting on an extra story on the present building, or would it destroy their architectural beauty ?

I think the architecture of these buildings is so refined that I would not like to change it. The question came up when the Western block wTas destroyed in 1898, and after much consideration I made up my mind that we would not put on another story.

I agree with the suggestion of the hon. member for Macdonald (Mr. Boyd) with regard to ripping out the partitions and putting a large crowd into one room. You would then have better supervision over them, you could get better results and. economize space.

It is wonderful how many men you can accommodate in a moderate space where space is expensive. I have never been in the Armour building, but I have been in large shipping offices, and in the Produce Exchange Building in New York. You see there a whole army of men working in a very moderate space. I am sure the space per man is not one-fourth of what is allowed in these buildings.

I think in the Canadian Pacific Railway offices in Montreal, only the superior officers have rooms of their own, and all the employees are located in a large room together. The suggestion is worth considering.
You see the same thing in large banks.

There was a plan mooted some years ago of building a bridge across the Rideau canal and getting access to some government property on the other side. I heard that was a plan of Sir John A. Macdonald ; has that been under consideration ?

I apprehend that the Geological Museum will be built in the Major's Hill Park. Then this question of building a bridge will probably come up. A few days ago some friends and myself went over the ground and we discussed that improvement.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Did the hon. Minister of Public Works ever consider the idea of providing quarters for our Speaker, Sergeant-at-Arms and chief messenger, outside this building, thereby giving more accommodation for members and committees ? At present I think that if he will look into the matter, he will find that nearly one-half, if not more, of the space in this building is occupied by officials of the House. I think that we ought to provide a suitable residence for our Speaker outside. That plan would be much cheaper than enlarging the building, as the minister proposes. The same way with the chief messenger and the sergeant. The members of both sides of the House at present lack accommodation. If we had the room occupied by these officials we would have all the accommodation we need. I think the government ought to consider that. The members have to spend three, four or five months here every year, and they ought to have some comfort ?

During the coming recess I will give my best attention to the necessity of having addi-

tional accommodation, and I will consider * the suggestions that have been made tonight by hon. members on both sides. My hon. friend from East York (Mr. Maclean) has a plan of his own that he has submitted to me, and which I think has the approval , of the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Haggart). Other members of parliament have made suggestions to me.
I think if the hon. gentleman's views were carried out they would give us increased accommodation. As far as the chief messenger is concerned, I think it is only proper that he should remain In this building. The Speaker, I presume, would have no objection to be located outside. I will not make any promise now, but I will carefully look into the suggestions that have been made.

One serious disadvantage arising from a discussion like this in the House, is that it adds immediately to the value of land in Ottawa. I happen to have had occasion recently to make some inquiries in an indirect way as to the value of certain land, and I was told it had increased during the last month in consequence of some statements made in this House as to the necessity of the government getting more land.
Are there any other private residences owned by the government except Rideau Hall in or near the city ?
No, we have no other residences.

I think then it would be well, if we are going to have a surplus next year of five or six mililon dollars, to build some private residences for the members of the government, either across the bridge or in some other convenient place, so that we may know where to find them. I do not know where they live.
. I suppose they are scattered all over the city. I would suggest that we have a Minister's Row across the canal, or some other place. Of course, you would have the nicest residence for the premier. I do not expect ever to be premier myself, but who ever should be premier would expect the nicest residence. Then you would go down by gradation to the lowest place, which, I suppose, would be allotted to the Minister of Public Works. I think it would be a very good idea, because they have to pay rent and perhaps an exorbitant rent for the buildings where they live. I think if the government owned these buildings, hon. gentlemen in opposition would be aspiring and expecting some day to live in them, and that would stimulate them still further. I think it would be an excellent plan, if you had the ground, and had the money to do it. It would cost the country less to have a nice colony of ministers pretty close to the buildings, and convenient,
so that members might call and see them when they come down.

Was there not some suggestion in regard to the Supreme Court building, as to locating it in a new place ? Would that not be a good site for additional premises ? While I am on my feet I also want to ask the hon. minister about an elevator. There was a question about an elevator to be placed in this building.

In the improvements that we are going to carry out, there is room not only for one elevator, but for two elevators, which are most necessary to have.
Lighting Dominion Public Buildings-Additional, $5,000.	[DOT]
How much does this make altogether for lighting public buildings ?
We have an additional number of buildings all over Canada, and this amount is necessary for the lighting.
How' much was there in the main estimates ?
And this makes $50,000?
Every dollar of this expenditure is controlled by the chief architect.'
I think these additional buildings were made to do duty for an increase in the main estimates.

These estimates are for this year only. The appropriation voted in the main estimates is short, and we must have that sum of money for this year.
Nova Scotia-Comeauville-Repairs to Breakwater-Revote of lapsed amount, $1,200.
Why was it not expended before ?

Because the accounts were not received until after the appropriation books for 18991900 were closed.
Ingonish, North Bay-Breakwater-Balance due contractor, &c., $10,800.
What is the etcetera ?

This is for the foreman of the work, and so on.
Parker's Cove-Extension of wharf (work done, including interest on balance due contractor, revote of $1,822, $1,950.
Where is Parker's Cove ?

In Annapolis county.
New Brunswick-St. John Harbour-Negro Point-Breakwater, $3,000.
Is this for repairs or construction ?

Rebuilding and repairs.
Quebec-Ste. Emilie Wharf-To complete. $2.000.
Where is this ?

In Lotbiniere county.
Ontario-Hawkestone-New Wharf-Work done, $502.20.	f	'
We had better leave this, as there are no Ontario men here.

There are only a few small items.
Mr, WILSON. I think you had better leave them as there is not an Ontario man in the House.
What do you want to pass ?

Simply the Ontario items. They are only small items, and not disputable.
Port Burwell-Harbour improvements, $15,000.
What is being done there ?

The work is going on. I have explained the whole thing already. I will have another amount in the supplementary estimates, on which my hon. friends can ask for explanations again.
Manitoba-General repairs and improvement to harbour, river and bridge works, $1,500.
Where is that money to be expended?
This is for general repairs, small things that we have to do, works here and there.

I think that in the supplementary estimates for this year larger sums should be brought down for improvements on Lake Winnipeg. A very large sum of money is being expended on the improvement of St. Andrews rapids on the Red River, about $750,000, and to get the full benefit of that improvement there are other improvements which should be made. The mouth of the Red river should be dredged. There is a sum of -$8,000 in the estimates which I would like to have increased to $15,000. in order that this dredging might be stopped ; as you are aware, the dredging of the mouth of the Red River has been going on for 18 years, and I believe that if $25,000, or even $15,000, were
placed in the estimates this work could be discontinued after another year or two. Steps should also be taken to deepen the Icelandic river, and some of the other rivers emptying into that lake.
When the St. Andrews rapids improvements are completed, the level of the lake will be raised to such an extent that it will not be necessary to have any more dredging done at all.
"What does the minister propose to do in regard to the petitions he has received asking for the lowering of the level of Lake Manitoba, and also for dredging where they are running a small boat ?
As the hon. gentleman (Mr. Boyd) knows we are completing works for lowering the waters of the lake and they will be done for August next. I hope they will be successful.
I myself forwarded some petitions about dredging portions of that lake and I would like to know what is the intention of the minister.

I am very sorry to inform my hon. friend (Mr. Boyd) that unfortunately we have no dredge available. I have instructed our resident engineer to see what the dredge used there by Mr. Lemoine is worth and whether it is capable of doing the work which my hon. friend (Mr. Boyd) asks for. If the dredge is a fairly good one and if too much is not asked for it, I will be able to comply with the request of the hon. gentleman.
Dredging-Quebec and Ontario, $20,000.
What is the explanation, of this ? We have already had a vote for this, and I suppose this extra expenditure is for extra work ?

No. The appropriation is short and we want this $20,000 to go on with the work up to the 1st July. This is to pay for the work of our own dredges, and also for the dredges wo hire. My department is simply flooded with demands for dredging and I am very sorry that we cannot comply with them all. 1 would remind the House that we are building several dredges for the maritime provinces, for Ontario, for British Columbia and for Quebec, and these dredges will enable us to do better and cheaper work. As every one knows, the department has been very badly equipped in the past in this respect.

I avail myself of this opportunity to call attention to the want of some dredging at Pointe Claire. There is a wharf there that we are indebted to the minister for, but the last time I was in Pointe Claire there was a demand for dredging In

order to reach the wharf. Will the minister make a note of that ?
I will not only make a note, but I will do the work, which is better.
That is very acceptable. There is also some dredging required at the St. Lawrence Boating Club near Dorval, and I think the club deserves to have the work done for it.
I understand that all the work asked for last year both by my hon. friend (Mr. Monk) and other friends of ours has been done. If there is anything else necessary I will do it with pleasure.

As the minister seems to be in good humour, I would like to know what his intentions are about dredging the Napanee river. I brought this up last year and had a promise from the minister that he would obtain sufficient information to make an estimate, but when the supplemen-taries were before the House the acting minister told me they had no such information, and they would have to get a survey before they could make an appropriation. The survey has been made now and I would like to know if the minister intends to have a sum in the supplementary estimates to dredge that river.
The survey has been made and we have now the necessary information. We have only a limited number of dredges at our disposal, but we can take the amount necessary out of the general estimates.
Will you put in a special vote for this ?
It is not necessary.

I know it is not necessary, but your engineer made an estimate of the cost and I think the usual course is to put an item of that kind in the estimates. I quite understand about the general vote, but if you intend to do any special work you generally put in an item for it.
It can be taken out of the general appropriation.
You are taking a very large amount for general dredging and I may look to it being done.
We are asking $15,000 more this year for general dredging.
All right.
May I ask what is the intention of the minister with reference to the River Scugog, near Lindsay ?
We did dredging last year. We thought we had done enough to comply with the demands made upon us; but I will take a note of what my hon. friend says, and look again into the question.

The department did some blasting there last year in the river bed. and the debris was piled on one side and completely obstructed the way to one of the important industries to the town of Lindsay, and it is still lying there. I am sure the minister only needs to have his attention drawn to it.

I am sorry that my attention has not been called to that before. I will have it attended to immediately.
Dredging-British Columbia. $5,000.
Has the hon. minister given instructions for the upper harbour of Victoria to be dredged forthwith ?
Instructions have been sent that as soon as the work at Tozo Rock is completed, the dredge will work in the upper part of the harbour.
I am told that the work will only cost $1,500. The dredge is not working at Tozo Rock at the present time, I am informed.
The new dredge which we are building is a sand suction dredge, which could not work in the harbour of Victoria.
Why ?
The chief engineer informs me that the nature of the soil would not permit of the dredge working there. That is a matter into which we can look again.

I think you had better, foi', if I am rightly informed, it is just the kind of material in which the new dredge will work. It is mud and silt. The amount which the hon. gentleman has for Victoria harbour is absurdly small. I hope he will see that a larger amount is spent there than has been spent in the past. It is a very important harbour, in whicii there is a large amount of shipping.

I say that as soon as the work of removing the Tozo Rock is completed, the dredge will work in the upper part of the harbour. More than that I cannot say.
Roads and Bridges-Ottawa City-Bridges over the Ottawa river, the slides and the Rideau canal and approaches thereto-Ordinary repairs, &c., $2,500.
Explain.

This amount is asked by the chief engineer

to make repairs to the Wellington bridge, the Sapper's Bridge, and the other bridges which are under the Department of Public Works.
How is the amount expended which is voted annuai'y as a contribution to the cits'- in lieu of taxes ?
The Minister of Finance is the proper person to answer that question.

The money is in the hands of a commission appointed by the government. Their practice is to prepare estimates of their appropriations and send them to the Governor !n Council for approval. Having obtained that approval, the expenditure of the money is entirely under their control, though the accounts are subject to the audit of the Auditor General, as required by the Act.

It occurred to me that it might not be undesirable to have some portion of that money expended on Sussex street, which is in a very bad condition. That street connects property belonging to the government at one end with property belonging to the government at the other end, and it is traversed a great deal by prominent people who come to Ottawa. If the hon. gentleman has ever attempted to go over it, he will agree with me that it is in a most disgraceful condition. I do not know whether the hon. gentleman has had any experience on a bicycle. If he could be persuaded to learn to ride, and go over that street as I have done on a conveyance of that kind, he would concur most heartily in the suggestion I am making.

I quite agree with my hon. friend as to the desirability of improving Sussex street, and I hope the commission and the city authorities will be able to come to an understanding by which it may be improved. But having left all such matters in the hands of the commission, we can only bring the suggestion to their attention. I sympathize very much with the object the hon. gentleman has in view.
Surveys and inspections, $16,000.

This is intended to cover the cost of a survey on the French river, with the view of obtaining the necessary information in order to have the improvement carried out which the vast majority of the country desire. A survey was made last month, and this is to pay the work done. There is a difficult question to be decided. Lake Nipis-sing has been raised five feet to drown the rapids we have to grapple with, and we have not sufficient information to know how Mr. TARTE.
many thousand acres of land may be grounded. By the moderate expenditure of $2,000,000 or $3,000,000, we will have a direct route from Chicago and Duluth to North Bay on Lake Nipissing, which is only 330 miles from the port of Montreal. When we have twenty feet of water from Duluth to North Bay, we will have the best route we ever had for our western trade. The survey was made by Air. Fraser, one of the engineers of the department, with the help of some others of our engineers. The report has only been prepared in a temporary way, but, perhaps, before the session is through, I may place it before the House.
There is one item relating to the post office which I would like, the committee to take up.
I have some matters to bring up when the post office items come on.

There will be supplementary estimates for next year, on which any discussion that the hon. gentleman may have can come up. This is only one item to clean up next year's supplemental estimates.
Post Office-To complete payments for post office service to June 30, 1901, $125,000.

I asked the officers of the department to make up a careful estimate of what would be required to meet the expenditures of next year, and these amounts are made up particularly on account of the increased services on the different railroads, especially in British Columbia, Alanitoba aud the North-west. The railway mail service is increased $53,000 over the estimates made : extra expenditure for ordinary land conveyances, $40,000 ; increased expenditure for mail bags, owing to general expansion of the business, $12,000 : stationery, &e., $20.000: and the item of $500 for telegrams, incurred particularly cabling in connection with the Pacific cable and South African business.
Does this effect the question we had up early in the session, as to the general results of the post office administration during the past year ?

It would, to some extent. Perhaps it would be more satisfactory if I laid on the Table an estimate made by the officers-you cannot give a complete return of the receipts until the completion of the year.
Will the hon. gentleman be good enough to bring the statement down to the latest date it is possible to furnish it for ?

Yes.

I think it was pretty well understood in the House that men in the service would be allowed their salaries while away in South Africa, and most of the departments have been able to pay, because they had taken a vote. But these gentlemen are paid partly by mileage, and the Auditor General would not pay without a special vote. This is estimated on the average of what they earned in the previous years.

I think we have done a fair day's work, and that even according to the Mulock Act, we have earned our money.
Some resolutions reported.
The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES (Hon. Sir Louis Davies) moved the adjournment of the House.
What government business will be taken up on Monday ?
Private Bills will occupy probably most of the time. If time allows, some of the government Bills on the paper will be taken up, and then supply.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.

speechtext: What supply ?

We shall go right on with the supplementary estimates and clean them up. If the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright) is able to be here, we shall take his estimates, which, when concluded, will nearly clean up the main estimates.
Will the government bring down the railroad subsidies at the beginning of next week ? The right hon. Prime Minister promised that all documents will be down by that time.
Some time during the week, the Prime Minister said.
speakername: The MINISTER OF MARINE AND FISHERIES.
